extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, referees, research administrators, and scholars of science policy interested in peer-review processes and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and reform of scholarly peer-review practices, including experimental studies to detect bias, measures of referee agreement, and institutional roles (editors, programme directors) that affect decisions. Emphasis on empirical designs that separate ascription/prestige effects from manuscript quality and on implications for openness vs secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: reliability vs innovative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to objectify the review process are likely to purchase reliability at the price of innovative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should weigh the cost that increasing objectivity and interrater reliability may have on detecting and nurturing innovative, high-risk work; avoid designs or policies that prioritize consensus at the expense of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manuscripts eliciting low interrater agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: More heuristic communication in journals could be achieved by publishing manuscripts that elicit the least reliable ratings (i.e., the lowest interrater agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divergent reviews (one enthusiastic, another rejecting) may indicate robust, provocative issues; consider mechanisms to surface and publish work that provokes disagreement rather than only those with consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascription / prestige bias (Matthew Effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees and editors are more likely to judge a manuscript favourably if its author is recognized as being famous, or located at a prestigious institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies and policy should explicitly test for ascription effects (author name/institution prestige) and consider blinding or other mitigations to reduce prestige-driven differential treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flawed-masterpiece hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: High-risk (innovative) papers are more likely to contain errors or controversial points and thus may be disproportionately rejected despite importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing peer-review outcomes, distinguish between rejection due to low quality and rejection due to innovation-associated imperfections; experimental designs should sample both low-risk and high-risk papers to test this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection: control for risk level of papers
rubrics_metrics.description: One might deliberately seek out low-risk and high-risk papers and resubmit them, comparing referee response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure resubmission studies stratify by paper risk/innovation level (e.g., methods novelty, controversial claims) so effects are not confounded by differing baseline error rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial (2x2) design to separate ascription from other variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2 x 2 experimental design varying author eminence and presented author identity can separate ascription from other influences (e.g., eminent paper presented with low-status name vs low-status paper with eminent name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factorial manipulations of author identity/status and original paper status to isolate prestige effects from content quality or regression artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate manuscript structural features (Mahoney findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small changes in how data are presented, presence/absence of data, or whether conclusions agree with data can strongly influence reviewer judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental manipulations should include presentation format, data inclusion, and framing of conclusions to assess their impact on reviewer decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure detection of prior publication / plagiarism ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many referees and editors fail to detect resubmitted or recycled manuscripts (plagiarism), as evidenced by low detection rates in experiments and documented plagiarism cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reviewers' ability to detect previously published material and consider systemic changes (e.g., databases, open records) to improve detection and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social incentives that suppress whistleblowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may recognize recycled/plagiarized manuscripts but prefer not to report them to avoid career damage or controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should consider career-defense mechanisms and institutional disincentives that lead to non-reporting; policies to protect whistleblowers and reduce retaliation are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs must detect mixtures of positive and negative intentional bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale regression analyses (e.g., Cole et al.) may not detect mixtures of favouritism and disfavouritism; particularistic experimental manipulations are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use study designs capable of revealing both positive and negative directional biases (not just average effects) — e.g., targeted manipulations, qualitative case histories, and particularistic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include reviewer perceptions surveys (e.g., Hensler)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys of reviewers show many perceive peer review as biased and identify specific weaknesses (favoritism, bias against innovators, opportunities for bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine objective measures with reviewer self-reports to contextualize observed behaviours and to gauge perceived fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess interrater agreement and its disciplinary variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consensus among referees varies widely across disciplines (smaller SD in 'hard' sciences; larger SD in 'soft' sciences); interrater agreement should be measured (e.g., standard deviation of ratings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report measures of agreement and examine discipline-specific norms; high variance may reflect paradigm diversity, incompetence, or mixed biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using citation counts as sole quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation (Science Citation Index) scores may explain only a small fraction of variance in success/funding and may not predict current proposal quality or grant success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on citation metrics as proxies for manuscript or applicant quality; use multiple indicators and experimental controls where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze role of programme directors and editors, not just referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and programme directors have the real power to make final decisions and may override or select reviewers strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies of peer review should include editorial/administrative behaviour, selection of reviewers, and decision-making processes rather than attributing outcomes solely to anonymous referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for coded language and ambiguity in review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers often use 'code words and modes of negative judgments' whose meanings can be interpreted inconsistently across editors and administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing reviews, account for indirect or euphemistic language and variability in interpretation; consider standardized reporting formats or coding schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against deliberate selection/manipulation of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Programme directors or editors may 'play funny games' — choosing overly generous or overly severe reviewers to obtain a desired decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit reviewer selection procedures, require transparency or justification for reviewer choices, and consider safeguards to prevent manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine secrecy vs openness in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Secrecy pervades peer review although science's norm is communality; secrecy has been justified as quality control but has not prevented fraud/plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the costs and benefits of secret vs open review practices, including impacts on accountability, detection of fraud, and nurturing of innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider peer-review effects beyond manuscripts (prizes, hiring, societies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review also governs awarding of prizes, election to learned societies, and hiring/firing decisions — areas susceptible to bias and political influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and reform efforts should extend to these other evaluative arenas, not restrict attention to manuscript peer review alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for particularistic studies to reveal personality and paradigm biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Only careful particularistic (case-specific) studies can reveal the extent to which personality conflict, rivalries, paradigm differences, and other sources affect peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement aggregate statistical analyses with focused case studies and experiments that manipulate particular features to detect specific bias sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 1: Obtain permission from original authors/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission was obtained in writing from nearly all senior authors and publishers to use original papers as test manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical and legal clearance (author and publisher permission) is important when resubmitting published work for experimental purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 2: Pose compelling, high-interest questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The questions raised command much interest; the question about detection could even be labeled daring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose research questions that are both meaningful to the community and provocative enough to test critical assumptions about peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 3: Emphasize the study's importance convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of the study is competently discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly articulate the significance and implications of findings for practice and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 4: Document claims and cite contrary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about the reviewing process and previous research are amply documented; contrary findings are reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive literature context, acknowledge conflicting evidence, and situate the study among prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 5: Use a naturalistic setting
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural setting was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, conduct studies in realistic editorial environments to improve ecological validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 6: Provide a good rationale for manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: A good rationale was presented as to why the manipulable independent variable was important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify experimental manipulations with theoretical and empirical reasons showing their relevance to reviewer behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 7: Describe journals, articles, and institutions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The journals, articles, and author institutions were well described; readers were told what the treatment was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent descriptions of materials and treatments so results are interpretable and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 8: Document prestige affiliation evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence was presented to document 'prestige' affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize and provide evidence for measures of prestige (citation rates, institutional standing) used in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 9: Guard against superficial detection of recycled papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors guarded against superficial detection of the papers without changing meaning or otherwise compromising the treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resubmitting, ensure that changes do not trivially cue detection while preserving treatment integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 10: Use an optimum time lag between publication and resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: An optimum time lag (18-32 months) was used — short enough to expect detection, but long enough to reduce reviewer recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select resubmission intervals that balance detectability and avoidance of reviewer memory effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 11: Provide a plausible mechanism for observed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors provided a plausible explanation (a description of the mechanism) of why prestige mattered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose and test mechanisms (e.g., ascription leading to tolerance of flaws) rather than only reporting empirical associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 12: Present convergent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Convergent evidence in support of the reviewer bias hypothesis was presented (e.g., greater agreement among reviewers for nonblind journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulate findings using multiple measures and comparisons (blind vs nonblind, interrater agreement patterns) to strengthen inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 13: Highlight conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors' 'conjectures' were called to the readers' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly distinguish between established findings and speculative interpretations to guide future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 14: Acknowledge limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some (but not all) of the study's limitations were pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about methodological and interpretive limitations and how they might affect conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millman criterion 15: Note implications and make suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some implications of the research findings were noted and suggestions were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss policy or procedural recommendations and propose directions for reform or further study.
